title: Wafer-level photonic integration as a thesis
body:
## The Economics of Conviction

Against $1.2 million in total fiscal-year 2025 revenue — almost entirely non-recurring engineering receipts collected in dribs across four quarters — POET Technologies spent $18.08 million on research and development. That arithmetic is not an accident of timing or a transitional quirk to be smoothed away in a footnote. It is the operating model. The company exists, at this stage of its life, as a research program funded by capital markets rather than customers, and the $313.4 million of cash and short-term investments on its December 2025 balance sheet is the reserve that keeps that program running.

The R&D line in isolation flatters nobody. A $16.1 per dollar of revenue ratio is the kind of number that would end a conventional company's life. But conventional operating-company metrics misread POET's position entirely. The more useful frame is R&D as a share of total operating expenditure. At roughly 42 percent of the $43.16 million in total operating costs POET incurred in FY2025, the research-intensity ratio sits in territory typically occupied by deep-platform development companies — firms that have decided to own a process architecture before the market decides whether that architecture wins. The $2.22 million of stock-based compensation embedded in that R&D figure signals, in the understated language of SEC disclosure, that the scientists and engineers building the platform are being retained partly in equity — a rational structure when cash preservation matters and the engineers believe in the upside.

What the cash actually funds is a multi-year engineering programme centred on a single architectural proposition: that wafer-level photonic integration — assembling laser sources, modulators, photodetectors, and optical filters into a passive substrate at the wafer level rather than the board level — is the structurally superior method for manufacturing the next generation of co-packaged optics engines. Every dollar of the $18 million annual R&D budget is, in effect, a wager on that proposition.

## The Venkatesan Credential

The intellectual core of the proposition sits with one person. Dr. Suresh Venkatesan joined POET as Chairman and Chief Executive in 2015 carrying credentials that matter precisely because of the technology's process-centric character. His prior work at Freescale, where he held the designation of Freescale Fellow for CMOS contributions, and subsequently at GlobalFoundries, where he led development at the 28-nanometre node, gave him deep familiarity with the manufacturing physics that determine whether a photonic integration scheme can be reproduced at volume with acceptable yield. That background is significant: photonic integration failures are rarely failures of physics and more commonly failures of process control, yield engineering, and the hard-won manufacturing knowledge that does not reduce neatly to published papers.

By the snapshot date, Venkatesan held over 25 US patents and was listed as co-author on more than 50 technical papers. The portfolio is heavily process-technology-led — patents covering the mechanics of how structures are made rather than only what they do. That is a deliberate defensive posture. Product-function patents are routinely designed around; process-methodology patents are harder to circumvent because the process itself is the innovation.

## The POET Patent Stack

The company's own patent estate — distinct from Venkatesan's personal academic and inventor-of-record positions — spans wafer-level photonic integration, passive substrate design, low-optical-loss assembly methods, and multi-component integration techniques covering the co-location of lasers, modulators, photodetectors, and wavelength-division filters within a unified package. The technology perimeter described in POET's 20-F annual filing is coherent: the patents appear to address both the structural arrangement and the manufacturing processes required to achieve it.

A precise count of POET's own issued US and international patents was not surfaced in the primary source materials available at the snapshot date, and the 20-F does not present a consolidated patent-count disclosure. This is a gap investors evaluating the IP defensibility thesis should press management to address directly. Patent counts are not by themselves informative — claim scope and prosecution history matter more — but the absence of even a headline count in the primary filings is a transparency data point worth noting.

## Engineering Geography

POET's physical engineering footprint is spread across three jurisdictions. The corporate headquarters in Toronto houses the executive and administrative functions. The operational centre of gravity for manufacturing development is POET Singapore Pte. Ltd., the subsidiary that operates the wafer-level photonic integration line and is the facility where the company's process-technology claims must ultimately be demonstrated at production-relevant scale. The 20-F also references operations in China and Malaysia, consistent with the supply-chain geography of the broader photonics industry in Southeast Asia.

R&D personnel headcount is not separately disclosed in the filings available at the snapshot date. Total headcount figures appear in the annual report, but the engineering-versus-administrative split is not broken out in the public filings reviewed here. That omission makes it difficult to benchmark POET's engineering team depth against peers, and it limits outside analysis of whether the $18 million annual R&D spend reflects a large but junior engineering team or a smaller group of experienced process engineers commanding market-rate compensation.

## The Strategic IP Question

The patent portfolio's commercial value hinges on two separate tests, neither of which has been settled as of mid-2026. The first is architectural-replication prevention: whether POET's claims are broad and defensible enough that Broadcom, Intel, or Marvell — all of which have substantial internal CPO development programmes — cannot replicate the wafer-level integration approach without licensing POET's intellectual property. The second is licensing leverage: whether hyperscalers designing CPO supply chains will find POET's integration platform compelling enough to qualify it, which in turn creates a royalty or component-supply revenue stream.

Both tests require the same underlying condition: that POET's approach is genuinely differentiated from the competing architectures and that the patents, when examined under adversarial conditions, hold their claims. Neither condition has been stress-tested at commercial scale by the snapshot date. The company has announced engineering collaborations and has generated NRE revenue from named and unnamed counterparties, but qualification in a production hyperscaler CPO programme — the event that would actually validate the IP perimeter — remained outstanding.

## The Scale Gap and What It Implies

The central R&D question, stripped of corporate framing, is a ratio problem. Broadcom and Intel each deploy an order of magnitude more capital against their photonic integration programmes than POET's entire annual R&D budget. POET's $18 million cannot compete on engineering volume. The company's path to a defensible competitive position is not R&D-spend parity; it is the combination of platform-IP specificity and customer-qualification execution. A well-scoped patent estate that covers the exact process steps hyperscalers need to adopt can be more durable than a larger but diffuse research programme spread across multiple architectural bets.

Whether POET's IP is in fact defensible at hyperscaler scale — whether the claims survive inter partes review, whether the process methodology patents hold under adversarial examination, whether the passive substrate approach proves sufficiently differentiated from competing interposer architectures — is the question the next 18 to 24 months will begin to answer. The $313 million cash position ensures that POET will be present for that answer. It does not guarantee the answer will be favourable.
